name: Go
intro: Learn Go on a 9×9 board: stones, liberties, capturing, atari and ko, then the ideas that decide games: scoring, two eyes, ladders, snapbacks and the opening.

units.name: How Go works
units.blurb: Stones, liberties, capturing, atari, and the suicide and ko rules.

lessons.title: How to play Go: the board and the stones
lessons.summary: Go in one minute: two players take turns placing stones on the points of a grid to surround territory. Learn the board and how a move works.
lessons.wrap: Place a stone, never move it. Next: liberties, the idea everything in Go is built on.

steps.text:
Go is played on a grid of lines. Stones go on the points where lines cross, not in the squares. Beginners use a 9×9 board; the full board is 19×19.

You play black and your opponent plays white. Black moves first.
On your turn you place one stone on any empty point. Once placed, a stone never moves. It stays until the end of the game, unless it’s captured.
steps.prompt: Place a stone on the centre point.
steps.wrong: The centre is the point in the very middle, five lines in from every side.

steps.text: The dots on the board are star points. They’re just there to help you find your way around.
steps.prompt: Tap all five star points.
steps.wrong: Look for the small dots printed on the board.
steps.done: All five. They make handy landmarks.

steps.text: The aim of Go is to surround more of the board than your opponent. You’ll learn exactly how it’s counted later.
steps.prompt: Can you move a stone after placing it?
options: Yes, one point at a time
No, stones stay where they’re placed
steps.explain: No. Stones never move. A stone only leaves the board if it’s captured.

lessons.title: Go liberties: how stones breathe
lessons.summary: Liberties are the empty points next to a stone. They decide everything in Go: a stone or group with no liberties is captured. Learn to count them.
lessons.wrap: Middle 4, edge 3, corner 2. Next: taking away the last one.

steps.text:
The empty points directly next to a stone (up, down, left and right) are its liberties. Diagonal points don’t count.

A stone in the middle has four.
Stones on the edge have fewer.
steps.prompt: Tap every liberty of the white stone on the edge.
steps.wrong: Only points joined to the stone by a line count, not diagonals.
steps.done: Three. The edge takes one away.

steps.text: And in the corner…
steps.prompt: Tap every liberty of the white stone in the corner.
steps.wrong: Follow the lines out of the corner stone.
steps.done: Just two. Corner stones are the easiest to capture.

steps.text: Stones of the same colour next to each other form a group. A group shares all of its liberties.
steps.prompt: Tap every liberty of the group of two white stones.
steps.wrong: Count around both stones, not just one.
steps.done: Six liberties for the pair. Connected stones are stronger.

lessons.title: Capturing in Go: taking the last liberty
lessons.summary: In Go you capture a stone or group by filling its last liberty. Practise captures in the middle, on the edge and of a whole group.
lessons.wrap: Fill the last liberty and the stones come off. Next: atari, when a group is down to one.

steps.text:
When a stone or group has no liberties left, it’s captured and taken off the board. Captures count towards your score.

This white stone has one liberty left.
steps.prompt: Capture the white stone.
steps.done: Captured. The point is empty again.

steps.text: On the edge, it takes fewer stones.
steps.prompt: Capture the white stone on the edge.
steps.done: Two black stones and one more were enough.

steps.text: A whole group is captured when the group runs out of liberties, all at once.
steps.prompt: Capture both white stones with one move.
steps.wrong: The pair shares its liberties. Find the last empty point next to either stone.
steps.done: Two stones off the board in one move.

lessons.title: Go atari: one liberty left
lessons.summary: Atari means a stone or group has just one liberty and can be captured next move. Learn to put stones in atari and to run your own to safety.
lessons.wrap: Put theirs in atari, rescue yours. Next: the two moves you can’t make.

steps.text: A stone or group with only one liberty left is in atari. It can be captured on the next move.
steps.prompt: Put the white stone in atari.
steps.wrong: Leave the white stone with exactly one empty point next to it.
steps.done: Atari! White has to do something about it now.

steps.text: Now it’s your stone in atari. One way to save it is to extend: add a stone on its last liberty so the group has more.
steps.prompt: Save your stone.
steps.wrong: Your stone has just one empty point next to it. Grow into it.
steps.done: Two stones together with three liberties. Safe for now.

steps.text: Check the idea.
steps.prompt: White has a group in atari. What can you do on your next move?
options: Nothing until it has zero liberties
steps.explain: Capture it, by filling its last liberty.

lessons.title: Go rules: no suicide, and the ko rule
lessons.summary: Two Go rules stop games going round in circles: you can’t play where your stone would have no liberties, and ko stops an instant recapture.
lessons.wrap: No suicide, and wait a move before retaking a ko. Next: the rules check.

steps.text: You can’t play a stone where it would have no liberties, unless it captures something. That would be suicide.
steps.prompt: Tap the one point black is not allowed to play.
steps.wrong: That point is fine. Look for an empty point completely surrounded by white.
steps.done: Right: a black stone there would have no liberties and capture nothing.

steps.text: Now look at this shape. Black can capture the white stone in the middle of the diamond.
steps.prompt: Capture the white stone.
steps.wrong: Find the white stone with only one liberty.
steps.done: Captured. But look: white could now take your stone straight back the same way…

steps.text: …and then you could take back, and so on forever. The ko rule stops this: after a single stone is captured, the other player can’t recapture straight away. They must play somewhere else first.
steps.prompt: White wants to retake the ko. When can they?
options: After playing one move somewhere else
steps.explain: After one move elsewhere. If black hasn’t fixed the ko by then, white may retake it.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Show you know the rules, then on to strategy.

lessons.title: Go rules check
lessons.summary: A quick Go rules check: count liberties, capture a stone and answer a question about ko. Pass it to unlock the strategy lessons.
lessons.wrap: Rules done. Now for what decides the game: territory, life and death.

steps.text: Three questions. First, liberties.
steps.prompt: Tap every liberty of the white stone.

steps.text: Second, a capture.
steps.prompt: Capture the white stone.

steps.text: Last one.
steps.prompt: Can you place a stone where it has no liberties and captures nothing?
steps.explain: No. It would be suicide, which isn’t allowed.

units.name: Life, death and tactics
units.blurb: Scoring, two eyes, ladders, snapbacks and the opening.

lessons.title: Go scoring: territory, stones and komi
lessons.summary: How a game of Go is scored: your stones plus the empty points you surround, with komi for white. Learn to count a finished 9×9 game.
lessons.wrap: Stones plus surrounded points, plus komi for white. Next: groups that can never be captured.

steps.text:
When neither player can gain anything, both pass and the game ends. Each player scores their stones on the board plus the empty points they surround. That’s area scoring, used here.

White gets komi, 6.5 points, to make up for black moving first.
Count this finished game. Black has 9 stones and surrounds 4 columns of 9 points. White has 9 stones and surrounds 3 columns.
steps.prompt: What are the scores?

steps.text: Now add komi.
steps.prompt: With 6.5 komi for white, who wins?
steps.explain: White has 36 + 6.5 = 42.5. Black wins by 2.5. The half point means Go games can’t be drawn.

lessons.title: Go life and death: two eyes
lessons.summary: A group with two separate eyes can never be captured. Learn what an eye is, and practise finding the vital point that makes two.
lessons.wrap: Two eyes means alive forever. Next: the ladder, a capture that runs across the board.

steps.text:
An eye is an empty point inside your group that the opponent can’t fill: a stone played there would have no liberties.

A group with two separate eyes can never be captured. White would need to fill both at once, and it only gets one move.
Your group in the corner has a space of three points. Right now it’s one big eye. White could play in the middle and kill it.
steps.prompt: Play the vital point to make two eyes.
steps.wrong: Split the space into two separate eyes. Which point divides it?
steps.done: Two eyes. This group will live forever.

steps.text: Check the idea.
steps.prompt: Why can’t white capture a group with two eyes?
options: Eyes are protected by a special rule
White can only fill one eye at a time, and a stone in either would be suicide
Groups in the corner are always safe
steps.explain: Each white stone in an eye would have no liberties and capture nothing, so it’s suicide. Both eyes would have to be filled at once.

lessons.title: Go tactics: the ladder
lessons.summary: The ladder is Go’s most famous capture: keep a stone in atari as it zigzags across the board until it hits the edge. Chase one down yourself.
lessons.wrap: Atari, atari, atari… until the edge. Next: snapback, the sacrifice that captures more.

steps.text: A ladder keeps a stone in atari again and again. Each time it runs, it still has just two liberties, so you put it straight back in atari. It zigzags across the board until it hits the edge and is captured.
Chase the white stone towards the bottom-left corner. Start with atari from the right, then keep putting it back in atari from the side that drives it towards the edge.
steps.prompt: Put the white stone in atari and keep chasing it.
steps.wrong: That lets white run the wrong way. Put it in atari from the other side.
steps.done: Caught at the edge. That’s a ladder.

lessons.title: Go tactics: snapback
lessons.summary: Snapback in Go: sacrifice one stone so that white’s capturing group is left with a single liberty, then take the whole group back.
lessons.wrap: Give one, take five. Next: where to play first on a 9×9 board.

steps.text: Sometimes the best move is to put a stone where it will be captured. If the stones that capture it are left with just one liberty, you take them all back. That’s a snapback.
White’s group in the corner has two liberties.
steps.prompt: Throw in a stone, let white take it, then capture the group.
steps.wrong: Play between white’s stones on the bottom edge.
steps.next: …but now white has one liberty. Take the group.
steps.done: Five white stones for one of yours.

lessons.title: Go opening on a 9×9 board: corners first
lessons.summary: Where to play first in Go: corners, then sides, then the centre. Learn why, and the best opening points on a 9×9 board.
lessons.wrap: Corners, sides, centre. That’s the Go path complete!

steps.text:
It takes fewer stones to surround territory in a corner, where two edges help, than on a side. The centre takes the most. So players usually go corners first, then sides, then the centre.

On a 9×9 board the centre matters more than on a big board, and the star points are good starting places.
You’re black, and the board is empty.
steps.prompt: Play a good first move: a corner point or the centre.
steps.wrong: Too close to the edge, or too far from a corner. Try a star point or the centre.

steps.text: Last question.
steps.prompt: Why are corners worth taking early?
options: Stones in corners can’t be captured
Two edges help you surround territory with fewer stones
The rules say you must start there
steps.explain: The two edges do half the work, so corner territory is cheap.
